```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = '#>', eval = FALSE)
```

Many APIs return a long result in pages. Some generated wrappers fetch all of
those pages for you in one call. This guide is for the person calling such a
wrapper. The maintainer who turns paging on for an operation should read
[configuration](configuration.html#fetch-every-page-in-one-call) instead. The
examples use a hypothetical client with a paging wrapper named `get_items()`.

## How to tell a wrapper pages

A paging wrapper has two extra arguments at the end of its signature, and its
help page documents both:

```{r signature}
get_items(kind, pageNumber = 1L, all_pages = TRUE, max_pages = 100L)
```

`pageNumber` is the API's own page argument. `all_pages` and `max_pages` are
added by the wrapper and control the paging. A wrapper without `all_pages` makes
one request, as it always did.

## The basic call

```{r basic}
items <- get_items('books')
```

The wrapper requests page 1, then page 2, and so on, one request after another,
and stops when a page comes back empty. You get the pages combined into one
value, in page order: one table if the client turns responses into tables,
otherwise one list of records. When the client builds tables, one page
(`all_pages = FALSE`) and all pages are the same kind of table, so code that
works on one page keeps working on all of them. Without tables, a single page
comes back as the API sent it, and the combined call returns one list of records.

## Start somewhere else, or fetch one page

The page you give is the page the wrapper starts from:

```{r start}
get_items('books', pageNumber = 3)                   # pages 3, 4, 5, ... to the end
get_items('books', pageNumber = 3, all_pages = FALSE) # page 3 only
```

`all_pages = FALSE` is exactly the wrapper without paging: one request, the
plain result, nothing added to it. Use it to look at the shape of the data before
you fetch everything.

## Limit how much you fetch

`max_pages` is the most pages one call will request (the default is shown in the
help page). Reaching it stops the call with a warning, because there may be more
data:

```{r limit}
items <- get_items('books', max_pages = 10)
#> Warning message:
#> Pagination truncated at max_pages
```

Each page is one request to the API, so a large `max_pages` on a big result can
mean many requests. Keep it small while you explore, and watch any rate limits the
API documents.

## Find out why it stopped

By default, the result carries a record of the paging in `attr(, 'pagination')`.
A wrapper generated with operation policy `pagination: {metadata: false}` omits
this attribute while retaining limit warnings and errors:


```{r reason}
attr(items, 'pagination')
#> $requests
#> [1] 4
#> $item_count
#> [1] 7
#> $stop_reason
#> [1] "empty_page"
```

| `stop_reason` | Meaning | Is there more data? |
|---|---|---|
| `empty_page` | A page came back empty. This is the normal end. | No |
| `completed` | The client's own rule said the last page had arrived (for example a `last` flag in the response). | No |
| `max_pages` | You hit `max_pages`. | Possibly: raise the limit or continue from a later page |

If a wrapper always stops at `max_pages`, its pages never come back empty, for
example because the API wraps the records in an envelope such as
`{"data": [...]}`. Tell the client's maintainer; the fix is a setting, not
something to work around in your code.

`requests` is the number of pages requested, including the empty page when one
ended the call, and `item_count` is how many rows or records came back. Check for
truncation like this:

```{r truncated}
paging <- attr(items, 'pagination')
if (identical(paging$stop_reason, 'max_pages')) {
  # The call started at page 1, so the next page is the one after the pages it fetched.
  more <- get_items('books', pageNumber = 1L + paging$requests)
}
```

The record is only added when `all_pages = TRUE`. It can be lost if you modify
the result with a function that drops attributes, so read it right after the call.

## What a table looks like

When the client returns tables, the column types are worked out once over all
the pages together, exactly as if the API had sent every row in one response. A
column that holds `"F"` on one page and `"MF"` on another stays text, and an
identifier such as `"007"` is treated the same on every page. See [calling a
wrapper with many inputs](batched-wrappers.html) for the same rule applied to
vectors of inputs.

## When something goes wrong

If any page fails, the call stops with that error and returns nothing, so you
never get a silently incomplete result. Problems that affect the whole call, such
as a missing credential, are raised before the first request.

A dry run (the client's dry-run option) prepares the first page's request and
returns it without sending anything.

## Paging and many inputs do not combine

A wrapper either pages or takes a vector of inputs; it does not do both. To page
through several kinds, loop yourself:

```{r loop}
results <- lapply(c('books', 'films'), get_items)
```

## For maintainers

Hooks run once per page, and an optional `post_combine` hook runs once on the
combined result. A `pre_request` hook must not change the page argument; see
[hooks](hooks.html#run-a-hook-on-the-combined-result-of-a-batched-wrapper).

## Reviewed cursor paging

Generated wrappers accept `pagination.mode: cursor` for a string query/path input,
or an explicit client input used by a complete request binding. Use the client
input for a POST facade whose request mapping places its cursor in the body.
No response field names or cursor locations are inferred.

```yaml
operations:
  GET /items:
    pagination:
      mode: cursor
      parameter: cursor
      next_cursor: cursor_next
      completed: cursor_done
      items: cursor_items
      metadata: false
      error_policy: partial
      warn_errors: false
      on_limit: cursor_limit
```

These reviewed client functions describe an envelope explicitly:

```r
cursor_next <- function(page) page$pagination$nextCursor
cursor_done <- function(page, state) identical(page$pagination$hasNext, FALSE)
cursor_items <- function(page) api_request_table(page$results)
cursor_limit <- function(state, limit) {
  warning(paste('Pagination stopped at', limit, 'pages'), call. = FALSE)
}
```

The next cursor is opaque: NULL or an empty string ends iteration. Repeated
nonempty cursors, NA, non-string values and multi-entry cursors abort before
another request. A NULL initial GET cursor and an empty
initial POST cursor retain their public defaults. `all_pages = FALSE` sends one
request and applies `items` to that response. Automatic paging retains each raw
page for `completed` and `next_cursor`, and combines the extracted items.
Table extraction runs inside the batching context so `api_request_table()` can
build types over all pages. A dry run returns the first prepared request.

`error_policy` defaults to `stop`; `partial` retains successful pages and `empty`
discards them after a request error. `warn_errors` defaults to TRUE. Credential
and other `specmill_call_error` conditions always abort. Extraction and cursor
callback failures abort as well; successful-response formatter failures inside a
client response policy can use the documented call-error class when they must
remain hard errors.

Limit warnings default to the existing pager warning. An `on_limit(state, limit)`
client function replaces that warning when the successful page count reaches the
limit, including completion on that last page. Set `warn_limits: false` to
suppress limit warnings. The callback owns any service-specific warning text.
Existing page-mode wrappers and their defaults remain supported. Client helpers
must include the current pager adapter and pagination companion before adopting
these controls; generated clients do not need specmill at runtime.

`stop_on_empty` defaults to TRUE. Set `pagination.stop_on_empty: false` when an
empty collection can still advertise a next page. The reviewed completion and
next-cursor callbacks then determine continuation; cursor validation, repeat
detection and `max_pages` still apply. This does not override `stop_on_short` in
the standalone companion.
